metadata.title: Spatially Common Sparsity Based Adaptive Channel Estimation and Feedback for FDD Massive MIMO

extraction_notes.note: Numbered equation (10) is an optimization formulation that the paper calls 'the optimization' and 'our problem'; retyped from equation to problem (confidence 0.9) by Hard rule 4, although the equation-retyping rule only names results.
claim or algorithm: the LS estimator (13) is introduced together with a cited assertion that it is unbiased and approaches the CRLB; kept as an external claim.
assumption or claim: the channel sparsity, common-support and block-fading properties are physically motivated modelling hypotheses stated in prose with numbered equations; typed as assumptions.
The CRLB and overhead derivations are running text; the result was taken as the final 'Therefore' sentence and the preceding text as a prose proof.
Table I (per-iteration complex multiplications of OMP, SP, SAMP, DSAMP) is not a node; its conclusion is captured in ClP9 and the per-operation costs in RP4.

The contribution list in the introduction, the prose walk-through of Algorithm 1 (choice of G_0=8), the oracle-LS benchmark remark after (30), simulation set-up paragraphs and figure-only results were left out as restatements or experimental description.
Many simulation results are visible only in figures (eps files absent); claims were extracted from the sentences that describe them, one of which carries a long footnote kept verbatim.

nodes.name: CS based adaptive CSI acquisition scheme
nodes.statement: item CS based adaptive CSI acquisition scheme: By exploiting the spatially common sparsity of massive MIMO channels within the system bandwidth, this scheme substantially reduces the required time slot overhead for channel estimation and feedback, where the required time slot overhead is only dependent on the channel sparsity level, rather than the number of BS antennas as in conventional CSI acquisition schemes.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item \textbf{CS based adaptive CSI acquisition scheme}: By exploiting the spatially
 common sparsity of massive MIMO channels within the system bandwidth, this scheme
 substantially reduces the required time slot overhead for channel estimation and feedback,
 where the required time slot overhead is only dependent on the channel sparsity level,
 rather than the number of BS antennas as in conventional CSI acquisition schemes.
nodes.clean_text: item CS based adaptive CSI acquisition scheme: By exploiting the spatially common sparsity of massive MIMO channels within the system bandwidth, this scheme substantially reduces the required time slot overhead for channel estimation and feedback, where the required time slot overhead is only dependent on the channel sparsity level, rather than the number of BS antennas as in conventional CSI acquisition schemes.

nodes.statement: item Closed-loop channel tracking scheme: By leveraging the spatially common sparsity of massive MIMO channels during multiple time blocks, this scheme can further reduce the required time slot overhead.

nodes.name: DSAMP algorithm
nodes.statement: item DSAMP algorithm: This algorithm leverages the spatially common sparsity of massive MIMO channels to jointly estimate multiple channels associated with different subcarriers. Compared with the conventional algorithms, such as sparsity adaptive matching pursuit (SAMP), subspace pursuit (SP) and OMP, the proposed DSAMP substantially reduces the required time slot overhead with similar computational complexity.
nodes.raw_latex:
\item \textbf{DSAMP algorithm}: This algorithm leverages the spatially common sparsity of
 massive MIMO channels to jointly estimate multiple channels associated with different
 subcarriers. Compared with the conventional algorithms, such as sparsity adaptive
 matching pursuit (SAMP), subspace pursuit (SP) and OMP, the proposed DSAMP substantially
 reduces the required time slot overhead with similar computational complexity.

nodes.statement: Due to S_a ll M, after coordinates accounting for the majority of the channel energy is achieved, the next iteration will include a virtual angular coordinate that is dominated by the AWGN. The first stopping criterion is designed to detect this situation and to terminate the algorithm when an appropriate number of virtual angular domain coordinates have been tracked.
